vignette:
Mr. Khan speaks of his life as if it were two separate books, bound together by necessity but written in different languages. The first book is short, a novella of his youth in his home country. He was a university student, full of politics and poetry, convinced he could help bend the arc of his nation’s history. That book ends abruptly in the middle of a chapter. It ends with the splintered wood of his family’s front door and the cold weight of a rifle butt against his back.

He spent two years in a cell he could cross in four paces. He never uses the word “prison”; he calls it “that place.” In our sessions, he describes the sensory details with a detached clarity, as if narrating a film. The perpetual dampness that seeped into his bones, the single, weak bulb that was either always on or always off, the metallic clang of a bowl slid under the door. Time dissolved into a grey fog, marked only by the shifting guards whose footsteps he learned to identify. He speaks of the interrogations not in terms of what was done to him, but in terms of the room’s dimensions, the texture of the wooden chair, the way the light from the hallway would silhouette the men who came and went. He survived by mentally reciting poems and equations, anything to keep his mind from fraying. Control was the one thing they had taken completely, and he fought for scraps of it in the privacy of his own thoughts.

The second book of his life began when he was released, a ghost blinking in the sudden sunlight. His family, fearing for his safety, arranged for him to leave the country. He arrived in a new world with nothing but the clothes he wore and a profound silence where his youthful idealism used to be. He met Fatima, his wife, a few years later. He found work in a warehouse, the kind of physical, repetitive labor that left him too exhausted to think. For forty years, he built a life. A house, two children, now grandchildren. He was a good provider, a quiet husband, a reliable employee. He built a wall around those two years, brick by sturdy brick.

But the past is not a story that stays in its book. It bleeds through the pages. The warehouse, his sanctuary of mindless work, became a landscape of triggers. The high, narrow aisles between canyons of stacked pallets feel like walls closing in. The sudden, deafening shriek of a forklift reversing sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he’s hearing a cell door slam shut. He eats his lunch alone, in his car, because the crowded breakroom, with its loud chatter and unpredictable movements, leaves him feeling exposed and overwhelmed.

At home, the performance of normalcy is exhausting. His wife tells me he checks the locks on the doors and windows three, sometimes four times before bed, a ritual he cannot skip. A few months ago, she dropped a ceramic bowl in the kitchen, and he threw himself to the floor behind the sofa, shouting something in his native language she didn't understand. He emerged moments later, face pale and slick with sweat, unable to explain the terror that had seized him. He has nightmares most nights, dreams of being trapped in small, dark spaces, and wakes up tangled in his sheets, his jaw aching from clenching his teeth.

He came to see me after an incident with his grandson. They were playing hide-and-seek, and the five-year-old boy, in a fit of giggles, locked him in the hall closet. The sudden darkness, the click of the lock, the confinement—it was instantaneous. He began hammering on the door, screaming, a raw, primal panic that terrified the child. When his wife opened the door, she found him slumped against the wall, weeping uncontrollably. It was the first time she had seen him cry in their thirty-eight years of marriage. He says he can no longer live with the ghost in his house, this silent, watchful stranger who was born in that cell and has followed him ever since.
